clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants in C19orf12; the same gene underlies mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN), a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.
First delineated in two sisters of Malian origin with juvenile-onset progressive lower-limb spasticity.

Childhood or juvenile onset spastic paraparesis and weakness, often accompanied by wasting (amyotrophy) of the small hand muscles, an unusual pairing that points to concurrent lower motor neuron or anterior-horn involvement.
Distal sensory loss, an axonal peripheral neuropathy and optic atrophy have been described in some affected individuals.

C19orf12 disease is a phenotypic continuum: SPG43 sits at the milder, spastic-paraplegia-predominant end, while more severe alleles produce iron-accumulation neurodegeneration with dystonia, parkinsonism and cognitive decline.
Routine brain MRI may be unremarkable in the pure paraplegia presentation; iron-sensitive sequences should be examined for pallidal and nigral iron if extrapyramidal features emerge.
Consider this diagnosis in consanguineous pedigrees showing spastic paraplegia combined with intrinsic hand-muscle wasting.
reference.pathophysiology: C19orf12 encodes a small, highly conserved transmembrane protein embedded in mitochondrial membranes (with reported associations to the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria-associated membranes) whose precise function remains incompletely defined but which is co-regulated with genes of fatty-acid biosynthesis and cholesterol metabolism, implicating it in mitochondrial lipid homeostasis and bioenergetics. Biallelic loss-of-function variants impair this lipid-handling and energy role, producing length-dependent degeneration of the corticospinal tracts; with more damaging alleles the same defect drives progressive iron deposition in the basal ganglia that characterises the MPAN phenotype. SPG43 therefore represents the spastic-paraplegia-predominant expression of a single C19orf12 disease spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN) and other neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation disorders (e.g. PANK2, PLA2G6)
SPG7 (paraplegin) — a mitochondrial complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia
SPG35 (FA2H), SPG46 (GBA2), SPG54 (DDHD2) and SPG56 (CYP2U1) — other lipid-metabolism complicated spastic paraplegias
Juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and distal hereditary motor neuropathy, given the prominent hand amyotrophy
Spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy and neuropathy syndromes
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) — early-onset complicated forms with cognitive involvement
additionalInvestigations: Next-generation panel or exome sequencing covering C19orf12, with confirmation of biallelic variants and family segregation
Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences (susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo imaging) to detect basal-ganglia iron
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise axonal neuropathy and any anterior-horn involvement
Ophthalmological review with optic-nerve assessment and optical coherence tomography
Neuropsychological or cognitive assessment where decline is suspected
Genetic counselling appropriate to autosomal recessive inheritance
redFlags: Emergence of dystonia, parkinsonism or cognitive and behavioural decline, suggesting evolution toward the iron-accumulation (MPAN) end of the spectrum
Rapidly progressive weakness with prominent hand wasting or bulbar signs mimicking motor neuron disease
New or progressive visual failure from optic atrophy
Recurrent falls and loss of independent walking
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive over years and many individuals remain ambulant into adulthood. Those whose phenotype broadens toward iron-accumulation neurodegeneration develop more disabling extrapyramidal and cognitive impairment, and life expectancy can be reduced in severe MPAN-type disease.
pitfalls: Attributing hand amyotrophy to a coincidental motor neuron disease rather than recognising it as part of C19orf12 disease
Omitting iron-sensitive MRI sequences, so early basal-ganglia iron and the link to MPAN are missed
Assuming a pure paraplegia label is fixed, when the phenotype can broaden with time
Overlooking recessive inheritance in small or apparently non-consanguineous families
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical and genetic reviews
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy addressing both lower-limb spasticity and small-hand-muscle wasting, with orthoses and adaptive aids
Surveillance for evolution toward mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration, with iron-sensitive brain MRI if dystonia, parkinsonism or cognitive decline emerge
Management of extrapyramidal features if they develop, using dopaminergic therapy for parkinsonism and anti-dystonic agents or botulinum toxin for dystonia
Ophthalmological review and low-vision support for optic atrophy
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary neurology, rehabilitation and, where iron accumulation develops, movement-disorder input
